---
title: "Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt"
description: >
  Translate existing IRT code into mirt with mirtify(), see what changes and
  why, and look up any function in the crosswalk.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Many people learn item response theory with one package and later want to
move to another. If your scripts were written for **ltm**, **eRm**, **TAM** or
**irtQ**, `mirtify()` rewrites them as **mirt** code. It reads the code
without running it, so the original package does not even need to be
installed, and it explains every place where the two packages differ.

```{r}
library(mirtverse)
LSAT <- expand.table(LSAT6)   # the LSAT data used in the ltm examples
```

## A first translation

Give `mirtify()` your code as a string, as the path to an `.R` file, or
unquoted inside `{ }`:

```{r}
mirtify({
  library(ltm)
  fit <- rasch(LSAT)
  summary(fit)
  factor.scores(fit)
  item.fit(fit)
})
```

Three things happen:

- **Model calls become `mirt()` calls with the same model.** `ltm::rasch()`
  estimates one common discrimination for all items, so the translation adds
  a `CONSTRAIN` line rather than using mirt's `itemtype = "Rasch"` (which fixes
  the slopes at 1 and frees the latent variance instead).
- **Follow-up calls on the fitted object are translated too.** `mirtify()`
  remembers that `fit` came from `rasch()`, so `factor.scores(fit)` becomes
  `fscores()` with the matching method (ltm's empirical Bayes scores are
  posterior modes, which mirt calls MAP).
- **Each difference gets a note**, written as a comment above the line. Turn
  them off with `notes = FALSE`.

Code that does not involve these packages is left as it is. Calls that have
no mirt equivalent are kept as comments, with a note on what to use instead.

## Running the translation

`run = TRUE` also runs the translated code and keeps what it creates in
`$env`, so you can check the results straight away:

```{r}
res <- mirtify("fit <- ltm::rasch(LSAT)", run = TRUE)
coef(res$env$fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
```

Use `file = "analysis-mirt.R"` to save the script, or `as.character()` to get
it as a string.

## eRm: conditional and marginal likelihood

eRm estimates Rasch models by conditional maximum likelihood (CML), while
mirt uses marginal maximum likelihood (MML) with a normal latent trait. For
the Rasch family the two give very similar item estimates. eRm reports item
*easiness* (minus the difficulty) centred to sum to zero, so translated
`coef()` and `summary()` calls convert mirt's difficulties to the same form.

```{r}
mirtify({
  library(eRm)
  fit <- RM(raschdat1)
  coef(fit)
  pp <- person.parameter(fit)
  itemfit(pp)
  LRtest(fit)
  plotPImap(fit)
})
```

Andersen's likelihood-ratio test (`LRtest()`) becomes the same comparison in
mirt: a model with equal item parameters in the low and high score groups
against one with separate parameters. On `raschdat1` eRm gives
LR = 32.5 with 29 df (p = .30) and the translation gives 32.8 with 29 df
(p = .29).

## TAM: Q matrices, groups and latent regression

`tam.mml()` and `tam.mml.2pl()` translate with their most used arguments: a
Q matrix becomes a `mirt.model()` with correlated dimensions, `group` becomes
`multipleGroup()` with equal item parameters and free group means and
variances, `Y` becomes mirt's latent regression (`covdata` and `formula`),
and `pweights` becomes `survey.weights`.

```{r}
mirtify("library(TAM)
         mod <- tam.mml(resp, Q = Q)
         mod2 <- tam.mml.2pl(resp, group = school)
         wle <- tam.wle(mod)
         wle$WLE.rel
         tam.modelfit(mod)
         IRT.compareModels(mod, mod2)")
```

## irtQ: the scaling constant D and priors

irtQ often uses `D = 1.702`, which multiplies every slope. mirt has no `D`,
so its slopes equal irtQ's times 1.702. The translated `summary()` and
`coef()` calls divide them back. The translation also keeps irtQ's defaults
that mirt does not share: 49 quadrature points from -6 to 6, one shared slope
for `1PLM` items, and a Beta(5, 16) prior on the guessing parameters.

```{r}
mirtify("library(irtQ)
         mod <- est_irt(data = resp, D = 1.702,
                        model = c('1PLM', '1PLM', '3PLM', '3PLM', 'GRM'),
                        cats = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 4))
         summary(mod)
         est_score(mod, method = 'WL')
         sx2_fit(mod)")
```

## How close are the results?

The package tests fit each model with the original package and with the
translated mirt code, then compare the estimates. These are the largest
absolute differences:

| Original call | Compared | Largest difference |
|---|---|---|
| `ltm::rasch(LSAT)` | difficulties, common slope | 0.001 |
| `ltm::ltm(LSAT ~ z1)` | difficulties, slopes | 0.001 |
| `ltm::grm(Science)` | thresholds, slopes | 0.006 |
| `ltm::gpcm(Science, constraint = "rasch")` | thresholds | 0.001 |
| `eRm::RM(raschdat1)` | item easiness (CML vs MML) | 0.005 |
| `TAM::tam.mml(data.sim.rasch)` | difficulties, variance | 0.001 |
| `TAM::tam.mml.2pl(data.sim.rasch)` | slopes, intercepts | 0.003 |
| `TAM::tam.mml(Science)` (partial credit) | log-likelihood | identical |
| `irtQ::est_irt(model = "1PLM"/"2PLM")` | slopes, difficulties | 0.006 |

The small differences come from the number of quadrature points (ltm uses 21
and TAM 21, mirt 61) and from convergence tolerances. Two cases differ more,
and the notes say so:

- **Polytomous Rasch models in eRm** (`PCM()`): eRm centres the item
  parameters and mirt centres the persons, so compare thresholds after
  subtracting their mean.
- **3PL models with a guessing prior in irtQ**: the likelihood can have more
  than one peak, so the two packages may stop at slightly different
  estimates. Compare the log-likelihoods if the estimates differ.

## What is not translated

A few functions have no direct mirt counterpart. `mirtify()` keeps them as
comments and says what to use instead: eRm's repeated-measures models
(`LRSM()`, `LPCM()`) and nonparametric tests (`NPtest()`), irtQ's
fixed-ability calibration (`est_item()`) and its list-based multiple-group
function (`est_mg()`), and ltm's modified parallel analysis (`unidimTest()`,
translated to `M2()` as a fit check). Arguments such as TAM's design matrices
(`A`, `B`, `xsi.fixed`) are flagged in the notes and the statement is marked
as translated with caveats.

## The crosswalk

`mirtify_crosswalk()` lists every function `mirtify()` knows:

```{r}
knitr::kable(mirtify_crosswalk())
```
